claim: Calcium-permeable AMPA-type glutamate receptors (CP-AMPARs) contribute to many forms of synaptic plasticity and pathology.
source: Calcium-permeable AMPA-type glutamate receptors (CP-AMPARs) contribute to many forms of synaptic plasticity and pathology.
evidence: This is a general statement about CP-AMPARs that is supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: CP-AMPARs can be distinguished from GluA2-containing calcium-impermeable AMPARs by the inward rectification of their currents.
source: They can be distinguished from GluA2-containing calcium-impermeable AMPARs by the inward rectification of their currents, which reflects voltage-dependent channel block by intracellular spermine.
evidence: This statement describes an established method for distinguishing CP-AMPARs based on their electrophysiological properties.

claim: The inward rectification of CP-AMPAR currents reflects voltage-dependent channel block by intracellular spermine.
source: They can be distinguished from GluA2-containing calcium-impermeable AMPARs by the inward rectification of their currents, which reflects voltage-dependent channel block by intracellular spermine.
evidence: This describes the mechanism underlying the rectification property of CP-AMPARs.

claim: The efficacy of spermine as a blocker is differentially altered by the presence of AMPAR auxiliary subunits including transmembrane AMPAR regulatory proteins, cornichons, and GSG1L.
source: However, the efficacy of this weakly permeant blocker is differentially altered by the presence of AMPAR auxiliary subunits – including transmembrane AMPAR regulatory proteins, cornichons, and GSG1L – which are widely expressed in neurons and glia.
evidence: This statement is supported by prior research knowledge about how auxiliary subunits affect spermine block.

claim: AMPAR auxiliary subunits are widely expressed in neurons and glia.
source: However, the efficacy of this weakly permeant blocker is differentially altered by the presence of AMPAR auxiliary subunits – including transmembrane AMPAR regulatory proteins, cornichons, and GSG1L – which are widely expressed in neurons and glia.
evidence: This is a statement about the expression pattern of auxiliary subunits based on established knowledge.

claim: The presence of auxiliary subunits complicates the interpretation of rectification as a measure of CP-AMPAR expression.
source: This complicates the interpretation of rectification as a measure of CP-AMPAR expression.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential effects of auxiliary subunits on spermine block.

claim: The inclusion of 1-naphthylacetyl spermine (NASPM) in the intracellular solution results in a complete block of GluA1-mediated outward currents irrespective of the type of associated auxiliary subunit.
source: Here, we show that the inclusion of the spider toxin analog 1-naphthylacetyl spermine (NASPM) in the intracellular solution results in a complete block of GluA1-mediated outward currents irrespective of the type of associated auxiliary subunit.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: In neurons from GluA2-knockout mice expressing only CP-AMPARs, intracellular NASPM completely blocks outward synaptic currents.
source: In neurons from GluA2-knockout mice expressing only CP-AMPARs, intracellular NASPM, unlike spermine, completely blocks outward synaptic currents.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from GluA2 KO mice.

claim: Intracellular spermine does not completely block outward synaptic currents in neurons from GluA2-knockout mice expressing only CP-AMPARs.
source: In neurons from GluA2-knockout mice expressing only CP-AMPARs, intracellular NASPM, unlike spermine, completely blocks outward synaptic currents.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data comparing NASPM and spermine.

claim: The block of CP-AMPARs by intracellular NASPM is unaffected by auxiliary subunit content.
source: Thus, our results identify a functional measure of CP-AMPARs, that is unaffected by their auxiliary subunit content.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by experimental data with various auxiliary subunits.

claim: AMPARs mediate the fast component of excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) throughout the mammalian brain.
source: AMPA-type glutamate receptors (AMPARs) mediate the fast component of excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) throughout the mammalian brain (Baranovic and Plested, 2016; Greger et al., 2017; Hansen et al., 2021) and their regulation allows lasting changes in synaptic strength that are essential for normal brain function (Huganir and Nicoll, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Regulation of AMPARs allows lasting changes in synaptic strength that are essential for normal brain function.
source: AMPA-type glutamate receptors (AMPARs) mediate the fast component of excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) throughout the mammalian brain (Baranovic and Plested, 2016; Greger et al., 2017; Hansen et al., 2021) and their regulation allows lasting changes in synaptic strength that are essential for normal brain function (Huganir and Nicoll, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: AMPARs are cation-permeable channels that exist as homo- or heterotetrameric assemblies of the homologous pore-forming subunits GluA1-4.
source: AMPARs are cation-permeable channels that exist as homo- or heterotetrameric assemblies of the homologous pore-forming subunits GluA1-4, encoded by the genes Gria1-4.
evidence: This describes the structural organization of AMPARs based on established knowledge.

claim: GluA1-4 subunits are encoded by the genes Gria1-4.
source: AMPARs are cation-permeable channels that exist as homo- or heterotetrameric assemblies of the homologous pore-forming subunits GluA1-4, encoded by the genes Gria1-4.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the genetic encoding of AMPAR subunits.

claim: A majority of central AMPARs are GluA2-containing di- or tri-heteromeric assemblies.
source: While a majority of central AMPARs are GluA2-containing di- or tri-heteromeric assemblies (Lu et al., 2009; Wenthold et al., 1996; Zhao et al., 2019), those lacking GluA2 constitute an important functionally distinct and widely occurring subtype.
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: AMPARs lacking GluA2 constitute an important functionally distinct and widely occurring subtype.
source: While a majority of central AMPARs are GluA2-containing di- or tri-heteromeric assemblies (Lu et al., 2009; Wenthold et al., 1996; Zhao et al., 2019), those lacking GluA2 constitute an important functionally distinct and widely occurring subtype.
evidence: This is a statement about the functional significance of GluA2-lacking AMPARs based on established knowledge.

claim: Editing of Gria2 pre-mRNA at codon 607 results in the substitution of a genetically encoded glutamine (Q) with an arginine (R).
source: Editing of Gria2 pre-mRNA at codon 607 results in the substitution of a genetically encoded glutamine (Q) with an arginine (R).
evidence: This describes a molecular mechanism of RNA editing in GluA2.

claim: The Q/R editing switch from a neutral to a positively charged residue in the pore-forming loop causes receptors containing Q/R edited GluA2 to have a greatly reduced Ca2+ permeability compared to those lacking GluA2.
source: This switch from a neutral to a positively charged residue in the pore-forming loop causes receptors containing Q/R edited GluA2 to have a greatly reduced Ca2+ permeability compared to those lacking GluA2 (Burnashev et al., 1992; Kuner et al., 2001; Sommer et al., 1991).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: GluA2 mRNA editing at the Q/R site is essentially complete.
source: As this mRNA editing is essentially complete, AMPARs are commonly divided into GluA2-containing Ca2+-impermeable (CI-) and GluA2-lacking Ca2+-permeable (CP-) forms (Bowie, 2012; Burnashev et al., 1992; Cull-Candy et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: AMPARs are commonly divided into GluA2-containing Ca2+-impermeable (CI-) and GluA2-lacking Ca2+-permeable (CP-) forms.
source: As this mRNA editing is essentially complete, AMPARs are commonly divided into GluA2-containing Ca2+-impermeable (CI-) and GluA2-lacking Ca2+-permeable (CP-) forms (Bowie, 2012; Burnashev et al., 1992; Cull-Candy et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CP-AMPARs have greater single-channel conductance than CI-AMPARs.
source: Aside from allowing Ca2+ flux, CP-AMPARs differ from CI-AMPARs in having greater single-channel conductance (Benke and Traynelis, 2018, Swanson et al., 1997) and susceptibility to voltage-dependent block by the endogenous intracellular polyamines spermine and spermidine (Bowie and Mayer, 1995; Donevan and Rogawski, 1995; Kamboj et al., 1995; Koh et al., 1995a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CP-AMPARs have greater susceptibility to voltage-dependent block by the endogenous intracellular polyamines spermine and spermidine than CI-AMPARs.
source: Aside from allowing Ca2+ flux, CP-AMPARs differ from CI-AMPARs in having greater single-channel conductance (Benke and Traynelis, 2018, Swanson et al., 1997) and susceptibility to voltage-dependent block by the endogenous intracellular polyamines spermine and spermidine (Bowie and Mayer, 1995; Donevan and Rogawski, 1995; Kamboj et al., 1995; Koh et al., 1995a).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: CP-AMPARs can be blocked in a use-dependent manner by extracellular application of polyamines.
source: They can also be blocked in a use-dependent manner by extracellular application of the same polyamines (Washburn and Dingledine, 1996) or various exogenous organic cations, such as the spermine analog N-(4-hydroxyphenylpropanoyl)-spermine (HPP-SP; Washburn and Dingledine, 1996), the polyamine-amide wasp toxin philanthotoxin-4,3,3 (PhTx-433; Washburn and Dingledine, 1996), the spider toxin analog 1-naphthylacetyl spermine (NASPM; Tsubokawa et al., 1995), and the dicationic adamantane derivative IEM-1460 (Magazanik et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CP-AMPARs can be blocked by extracellular application of various exogenous organic cations including HPP-SP, PhTx-433, NASPM, and IEM-1460.
source: They can also be blocked in a use-dependent manner by extracellular application of the same polyamines (Washburn and Dingledine, 1996) or various exogenous organic cations, such as the spermine analog N-(4-hydroxyphenylpropanoyl)-spermine (HPP-SP; Washburn and Dingledine, 1996), the polyamine-amide wasp toxin philanthotoxin-4,3,3 (PhTx-433; Washburn and Dingledine, 1996), the spider toxin analog 1-naphthylacetyl spermine (NASPM; Tsubokawa et al., 1995), and the dicationic adamantane derivative IEM-1460 (Magazanik et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Block of CP-AMPARs by intracellular polyamines results in inwardly- or bi-rectifying current-voltage relationships.
source: Block of CP-AMPARs by intracellular polyamines results in inwardly- or bi-rectifying current-voltage relationships.
evidence: This describes the electrophysiological consequence of polyamine block based on established knowledge.

claim: Rectification has been utilized extensively to identify the presence of CP-AMPARs in neurons.
source: This characteristic rectification – seen during whole-cell patch-clamp recordings in the presence of residual endogenous polyamines or added exogenous spermine – has been utilized extensively to identify the presence of CP-AMPARs in neurons.
evidence: This statement describes a widely used experimental approach in the field.

claim: Rectification has enabled the identification of cell- and synapse-specific CP-AMPAR expression.
source: Importantly, this approach has enabled the identification of cell- and synapse-specific CP-AMPAR expression (Koh et al., 1995b, Tóth and McBain, 1998), changes in CP-AMPAR prevalence during development (Brill and Huguenard, 2008; Kumar et al., 2002; Soto et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2010), and roles for CP-AMPARs in multiple synaptic plasticities, including long-term potentiation (LTP) and depression (LTD) (Fortin et al., 2010; Lamsa et al., 2000; Liu and Cull-Candy, 2000; Mahanty and Sah, 1998; Manz et al., 2020; Plant et al., 2006; Sanderson et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Rectification has enabled the identification of changes in CP-AMPAR prevalence during development.
source: Importantly, this approach has enabled the identification of cell- and synapse-specific CP-AMPAR expression (Koh et al., 1995b, Tóth and McBain, 1998), changes in CP-AMPAR prevalence during development (Brill and Huguenard, 2008; Kumar et al., 2002; Soto et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2010), and roles for CP-AMPARs in multiple synaptic plasticities, including long-term potentiation (LTP) and depression (LTD) (Fortin et al., 2010; Lamsa et al., 2000; Liu and Cull-Candy, 2000; Mahanty and Sah, 1998; Manz et al., 2020; Plant et al., 2006; Sanderson et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Rectification has enabled the identification of roles for CP-AMPARs in multiple synaptic plasticities, including long-term potentiation (LTP) and depression (LTD).
source: Importantly, this approach has enabled the identification of cell- and synapse-specific CP-AMPAR expression (Koh et al., 1995b, Tóth and McBain, 1998), changes in CP-AMPAR prevalence during development (Brill and Huguenard, 2008; Kumar et al., 2002; Soto et al., 2007; Yang et al., 2010), and roles for CP-AMPARs in multiple synaptic plasticities, including long-term potentiation (LTP) and depression (LTD) (Fortin et al., 2010; Lamsa et al., 2000; Liu and Cull-Candy, 2000; Mahanty and Sah, 1998; Manz et al., 2020; Plant et al., 2006; Sanderson et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Rectification has suggested CP-AMPAR changes associated with various conditions, including ischemia, brain trauma, schizophrenia, stress, and glaucoma.
source: In addition, its use has suggested CP-AMPAR changes associated with various conditions, including ischemia (Dixon et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2004; Peng et al., 2006), brain trauma (Korgaonkar et al., 2020), schizophrenia (Druart et al., 2021), stress (Kuniishi et al., 2020), and glaucoma (Sladek and Nawy, 2020), and in circuit remodeling associated with fear-related behaviors (Clem and Huganir, 2010; Liu et al., 2010), drug addiction (Bellone and Lüscher, 2006; Conrad et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2013; Parrilla-Carrero et al., 2021; Scheyer et al., 2014; Van den Oever et al., 2008), and neuropathic or inflammatory pain (Goffer et al., 2013; Katano et al., 2008; Park et al., 2009; Sullivan et al., 2017; Vikman et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

source: In addition, its use has suggested CP-AMPAR changes associated with various conditions, including ischemia (Dixon et al., 2009; Liu et al., 2004; Peng et al., 2006), brain trauma (Korgaonkar et al., 2020), schizophrenia (Druart et al., 2021), stress (Kuniishi et al., 2020), and glaucoma (Sladek and Nawy, 2020), and in circuit remodeling associated with fear-related behaviors (Clem and Huganir, 2010; Liu et al., 2010), drug addiction (Bellone and Lüscher, 2006; Conrad et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2013; Parrilla-Carrero et al., 2021; Scheyer et al., 2014; Van den Oever et al., 2008), and neuropathic or inflammatory pain (Goffer et al., 2013; Katano et al., 2008; Park et al., 2009; Sullivan et al., 2017; Vikman et al., 2008).

claim: Native AMPARs co-assemble with various transmembrane auxiliary subunits that influence receptor biogenesis, synaptic targeting, and function.
source: Native AMPARs co-assemble with various transmembrane auxiliary subunits that influence receptor biogenesis, synaptic targeting, and function (Greger et al., 2017; Jackson and Nicoll, 2011b, Schwenk et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: TARPs and cornichons modify the block of CP-AMPARs by intracellular spermine by reducing inward rectification.
source: Importantly, several of these, including transmembrane AMPAR regulatory proteins (TARPs), cornichons, and germ cell-specific gene 1-like protein (GSG1L), have been shown to modify the block of CP-AMPARs by intracellular spermine. In the case of TARPs and CNIHs inward rectification is reduced (Brown et al., 2018; Cho et al., 2007; Coombs et al., 2012; Soto et al., 2007; Soto et al., 2009), whereas with GSG1L the rectification is increased (McGee et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: GSG1L modifies the block of CP-AMPARs by intracellular spermine by increasing rectification.
source: Importantly, several of these, including transmembrane AMPAR regulatory proteins (TARPs), cornichons, and germ cell-specific gene 1-like protein (GSG1L), have been shown to modify the block of CP-AMPARs by intracellular spermine. In the case of TARPs and CNIHs inward rectification is reduced (Brown et al., 2018; Cho et al., 2007; Coombs et al., 2012; Soto et al., 2007; Soto et al., 2009), whereas with GSG1L the rectification is increased (McGee et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Intracellular NASPM, PhTx-433, and PhTx-74 can be used to specifically and voltage-dependently block recombinant CP-AMPARs.
source: Here, we show that intracellular NASPM, PhTx-433, and PhTx-74 can be used to specifically and voltage-dependently block recombinant CP-AMPARs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Unlike spermine, intracellular NASPM, PhTx-433, and PhTx-74 allow negligible outward current at positive potentials.
source: Unlike spermine, which is permeant, these blockers allow negligible outward current at positive potentials.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: Spermine is a permeant blocker of CP-AMPARs.
source: Unlike spermine, which is permeant, these blockers allow negligible outward current at positive potentials.
evidence: This statement is based on established knowledge about spermine's properties.

claim: At +60 mV, 10 µM intracellular NASPM produces a use-dependent block of CP-AMPARs.
source: At +60 mV, 10 µM intracellular NASPM produces a use-dependent block, while at 100 µM it fully blocks outward currents in a use-independent manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: At +60 mV, 100 µM intracellular NASPM fully blocks outward currents from CP-AMPARs in a use-independent manner.
source: At +60 mV, 10 µM intracellular NASPM produces a use-dependent block, while at 100 µM it fully blocks outward currents in a use-independent manner.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data.

claim: The block of CP-AMPARs by 100 µM intracellular NASPM is unaffected by the presence of auxiliary subunits.
source: Critically, this block is unaffected by the presence of auxiliary subunits.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data with various auxiliary subunits.

claim: In three neuronal populations from GluA2-knockout mice, 100 µM intracellular NASPM causes full rectification of glutamate-evoked currents from extrasynaptic and synaptic CP-AMPARs.
source: Furthermore, in three neuronal populations from GluA2-knockout (GluA2 KO) mice (Jia et al., 1996), known to express different auxiliary proteins (Fukaya et al., 2006; Khodosevich et al., 2014; Tomita et al., 2003; Yamazaki et al., 2010), we show that 100 µM intracellular NASPM causes full rectification of glutamate-evoked currents from extrasynaptic and synaptic CP-AMPARs, something that cannot be achieved with spermine.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from GluA2 KO mice.

claim: Full rectification of glutamate-evoked currents from extrasynaptic and synaptic CP-AMPARs cannot be achieved with spermine in neuronal populations from GluA2-knockout mice.
source: Furthermore, in three neuronal populations from GluA2-knockout (GluA2 KO) mice (Jia et al., 1996), known to express different auxiliary proteins (Fukaya et al., 2006; Khodosevich et al., 2014; Tomita et al., 2003; Yamazaki et al., 2010), we show that 100 µM intracellular NASPM causes full rectification of glutamate-evoked currents from extrasynaptic and synaptic CP-AMPARs, something that cannot be achieved with spermine.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data comparing NASPM and spermine.

claim: The use of intracellular NASPM provides a simple and effective method for determining the relative contribution of CP-AMPARs to AMPAR-mediated currents, regardless of their associated auxiliary subunits.
source: Together, our results reveal that the use of intracellular NASPM provides a simple and effective method for determining the relative contribution of CP-AMPARs to AMPAR-mediated currents, regardless of their associated auxiliary subunits.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: In the absence of intracellular polyamines, homomeric GluA1 receptors generate outward currents at positive potentials, showing clear outward rectification.
source: As expected (McGee et al., 2015; Soto et al., 2007), in the absence of intracellular polyamines homomeric GluA1 receptors generated outward currents at positive potentials, showing clear outward rectification, while in the presence of 100 μM spermine, they displayed doubly rectifying responses (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data and citations to prior research.

claim: In the presence of 100 μM spermine, homomeric GluA1 receptors display doubly rectifying responses.
source: As expected (McGee et al., 2015; Soto et al., 2007), in the absence of intracellular polyamines homomeric GluA1 receptors generated outward currents at positive potentials, showing clear outward rectification, while in the presence of 100 μM spermine, they displayed doubly rectifying responses (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data and citations to prior research.

claim: When the intracellular solution contains 100 μM NASPM, GluA1 receptors display inwardly rectifying responses with negligible current passed at positive potentials.
source: By contrast, when the intracellular solution contained 100 μM NASPM, GluA1 receptors displayed inwardly rectifying responses with negligible current passed at positive potentials (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data presented in Figure 1b.

claim: Currents from GluA1/2 receptors in the presence of NASPM are non-rectifying.
source: Unlike responses from GluA1 alone, currents from GluA1/2 receptors in the presence of NASPM were non-rectifying (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data presented in Figure 1b.

claim: When added to the intracellular solution at 100 μM, each blocker (spermine, NASPM, PhTx-433, PhTx-74) confers marked inward rectification on the currents mediated by GluA1.
source: I-V plots showed that, when added to the intracellular solution at 100 μM, each blocker conferred marked inward rectification on the currents mediated by GluA1 (rectification index, RI+60/−60 0.02–0.26), but not on those mediated by GluA1/2 (RI+60/−60 0.84–1.30) (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data presented in Figure 1c.

claim: When added to the intracellular solution at 100 μM, the blockers (spermine, NASPM, PhTx-433, PhTx-74) do not confer marked inward rectification on currents mediated by GluA1/2.
source: I-V plots showed that, when added to the intracellular solution at 100 μM, each blocker conferred marked inward rectification on the currents mediated by GluA1 (rectification index, RI+60/−60 0.02–0.26), but not on those mediated by GluA1/2 (RI+60/−60 0.84–1.30) (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data presented in Figure 1c.

claim: The blockers (spermine, NASPM, PhTx-433, PhTx-74) produce selective voltage-dependent block of GluA2-lacking CP-AMPARs.
source: Thus, although differing in structure, they all produced selective voltage-dependent block of the GluA2-lacking CP-AMPARs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing differential effects on GluA1 vs GluA1/2.

claim: The block by intracellular PhTx-74 is restricted to CP-AMPARs, despite the fact that it produces low-affinity block of CI-AMPARs when applied extracellularly.
source: Of note, the block by intracellular PhTx-74 was restricted to CP-AMPARs, despite the fact that it produces low-affinity block of CI-AMPARs when applied extracellularly (Jackson et al., 2011b; Nilsen and England, 2007).
evidence: This is an observation from the study supported by data and citations to prior research.

claim: As the concentration of added blocker is increased (from 0.1 or 1 μM to 500 μM) there is a progressive negative shift in Vb (the potential at which 50% block occurs).
source: This revealed that as the concentration of added blocker was increased (from 0.1 or 1 μM to 500 μM) there was a progressive negative shift in Vb (the potential at which 50% block occurs) (Figure 2a and b).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data presented in Figure 2a and b.

claim: For steady-state conditions, the order of potency for the GluA1 block is spermine >NASPM >PhTx-433 >PhTx-74.
source: This showed that, for steady-state conditions, the order of potency for the GluA1 block was spermine >NASPM >PhTx-433 >PhTx-74 (Figure 2b and c).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from analysis of experimental data presented in Figure 2b and c.

claim: The potency of each blocker is reduced when GluA1 is co-expressed with TARP γ2 (between 7- and 18-fold reduction).
source: The same analysis demonstrated that the potency of each blocker was reduced when GluA1 was co-expressed with TARP γ2 (between 7- and 18-fold reduction; Figure 2b and c).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data presented in Figure 2b and c.

claim: For both peak and steady-state currents, the RI+60/−60 values obtained with 10 μM NASPM are less than those obtained with 10 μM spermine in GluA1/γ2 receptors.
source: For both peak and steady-state currents the RI+60/−60 values obtained with NASPM were less than those obtained with spermine. For peak current, RI+60/−60 was 0.37 ± 0.04 for NASPM and 0.56 ± 0.07 for spermine (n=11 and 10, respectively; unpaired mean difference −0.19 [−0.34,–0.045], p=0.031, two-sided Welch two-sample t-test). For steady-state current, RI+60/−60 was 0.04 ± 0.02 for NASPM and 0.90 ± 0.14 for spermine (n=8 and 7), respectively (unpaired mean difference −0.86 [−1.12,–0.62], p=0.00075).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by statistical analysis of data.

claim: G-V relationships determined from peak responses in the presence of 10 μM spermine or NASPM are largely overlapping in GluA1/γ2 receptors.
source: This difference was also evident in the G-V relationships; those determined from peak responses in the presence of spermine or NASPM were largely overlapping, while those from steady-state responses were markedly different at potentials positive to +40 mV, with a large outward conductance seen in the presence of spermine but not NASPM (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data presented in Figure 3b.

claim: G-V relationships from steady-state responses in the presence of 10 μM spermine or NASPM are markedly different at potentials positive to +40 mV in GluA1/γ2 receptors, with a large outward conductance seen in the presence of spermine but not NASPM.
source: This difference was also evident in the G-V relationships; those determined from peak responses in the presence of spermine or NASPM were largely overlapping, while those from steady-state responses were markedly different at potentials positive to +40 mV, with a large outward conductance seen in the presence of spermine but not NASPM (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data presented in Figure 3b.

claim: Intracellular spermine is a weakly permeable open-channel blocker of both CP-AMPARs and kainate receptors (KARs).
source: Intracellular spermine is a weakly permeable open-channel blocker of both CP-AMPARs and kainate receptors (KARs) (Bowie et al., 1998; Brown et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: For GluK2(Q) KARs, permeation of intracellular polyamines varies with molecular size, with HPP-SP and PhTx-433 showing little or no detectable relief from the block with depolarization.
source: However, for GluK2(Q) KARs, permeation of intracellular polyamines has been shown to vary with molecular size, with two molecules of greater width than spermine – N-(4-hydroxyphenylpropanoyl)-spermine (HPP-SP) and PhTx-433 – showing little or no detectable relief from the block with depolarization (Bähring et al., 1997).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: NASPM, with its naphthyl headgroup, displays limited permeability of CP-AMPAR channels.
source: We reasoned that NASPM, with its naphthyl headgroup, might also be expected to display limited permeability of CP-AMPAR channels. This could account for the shape of the ramp I-V (Figure 1c) and G-V plots with NASPM (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on reasoning from prior knowledge and their experimental observations.

claim: The pronounced effect of 10 μM intracellular NASPM on steady-state GluA1/γ2 currents at positive potentials is consistent with limited permeation, leading to the accumulation of channel block.
source: Indeed, the pronounced effect of 10 μM intracellular NASPM on steady-state GluA1/γ2 currents at positive potentials (Figure 3a) is also consistent with limited permeation, leading to the accumulation of channel block.
evidence: This is an interpretation of experimental data based on the hypothesis of limited permeation.

claim: The decay of GluA1/γ2 currents recorded in the presence of 10 μM NASPM is strongly voltage-dependent.
source: In line with this, we found that the decay of GluA1/γ2 currents recorded in the presence of NASPM was strongly voltage-dependent (Figure 3a and c).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data presented in Figure 3a and c.

claim: At negative potentials, τdecay values are similar in the presence and absence of 10 μM NASPM in GluA1/γ2 receptors.
source: At negative potentials, τdecay values were similar in the presence and absence of NASPM.
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data.

claim: At positive potentials (from +10 to +80 mV) the kinetics of GluA1/γ2 current decay in the presence and absence of 10 μM NASPM differ markedly.
source: However, at positive potentials (from +10 to +80 mV) the kinetics in the two conditions differed markedly. In the absence of NASPM current decay was slowed at positive potentials, while in the presence of NASPM, the decay was progressively accelerated (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by data presented in Figure 3d.

claim: In the absence of NASPM, τdecay of GluA1/γ2 currents is slower at +60 mV than at −60 mV.
source: In the absence of NASPM, τdecay was slower at +60 mV than at −60 mV (7.3 ± 0.6 ms versus 5.7 ± 0.3 ms, n=8; paired mean difference 1.55 ms [0.86, 2.62], p=0.019 two-sided paired Welch t-test).
evidence: This is an experimental observation supported by statistical analysis of data.

claim: In the presence of 10 μM NASPM, τdecay of GluA1/γ2 currents is markedly faster at +60 mV than at −60 mV.
